meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Beauty in things exists in the mind which contemplates them'?
meta.ogDescription: Genuinely David Hume, from "Of the Standard of Taste" (1757) — though the popular wording trims and rearranges his real sentence.

answer.label: Written by
answer.sourceLine: The thought — and most of the words — are genuinely Hume’s, from his essay “Of the Standard of Taste” (first published 1757 in Four Dissertations). His actual sentence runs: “Beauty is no quality in things themselves: It exists merely in the mind which contemplates them; and each mind perceives a different beauty.” The circulating short form compresses that into “Beauty in things exists in the mind which contemplates them” — the same idea, with the clause “exists…in the mind which contemplates them” kept verbatim.

source.excerpt: Beauty is no quality in things themselves: It exists merely in the mind which contemplates them; and each mind perceives a different beauty. One person may even perceive deformity, where another is sensible of beauty; and every individual ought to acquiesce in his own sentiment, without pretending to regulate those of others.
trail: The authoritative scholarly text at davidhume.org carries the sentence verbatim: “Beauty is no quality in things themselves: It exists merely in the mind which contemplates them.”
The Online Library of Liberty reproduces the same sentence and attributes it to “Of the Standard of Taste” in Essays, Moral, Political, Literary.
The trimmed form — “Beauty in things exists in the mind which contemplates them” — is what circulates on aggregators like Goodreads and BrainyQuote, credited to Hume.
source.excerptNote: Hume’s full sentence from “Of the Standard of Taste.” The popular quote keeps the middle clause and drops the opening negation — “Beauty is no quality in things themselves” — which is the very point Hume was making.

author.name: David Hume
author.heading: About David Hume
author.bio: David Hume (1711–1776) was a central figure of the Scottish Enlightenment, best known for his empiricism and skepticism in works like A Treatise of Human Nature and An Enquiry Concerning Human Understanding. In his essay “Of the Standard of Taste” he argued that beauty is not an objective property of things but a sentiment in the mind of the beholder — a founding statement of modern aesthetic subjectivism.

misattribution.heading: Right author, trimmed words
misattribution.intro: This one isn’t a fake — it’s a genuine Hume line that lost some words on its way through the quote sites.

items.why: Hume actually wrote “Beauty is no quality in things themselves: It exists merely in the mind which contemplates them.” The circulating version — “Beauty in things exists in the mind which contemplates them” — drops the opening negation and folds the two clauses together. See the verbatim text at davidhume.org.

The trimmed phrase “Beauty in things…” slightly muddies Hume’s point, which was precisely that beauty is not in things but only in the mind that contemplates them — his classic statement of aesthetic subjectivism in “Of the Standard of Taste”.

misattribution.truthLine: The attribution to Hume is correct and the source is real — his 1757 essay “Of the Standard of Taste”; only the exact phrasing has been shortened.

context.heading: Why it mattered
lead: Hume made this remark not as a throwaway compliment to beauty but to set up a genuine puzzle: if beauty is only a feeling in the mind, and every mind feels differently, how can we ever say one judgment of taste is better than another? “Of the Standard of Taste” is his attempt to answer that — to reconcile the subjectivity of beauty with the everyday conviction that some critics really do have better taste than others.
His solution points to the verdicts of experienced, unprejudiced critics as a practical standard, even though beauty itself remains a sentiment rather than a property of the object.
